Nilesh, sit down, I see that face. They called you boring at the party, didn't they? Let me tell you about your Avni aunty at nineteen, in the hostel in Pune. My roommates had a bottle every Saturday. First they offered. Then they teased. "Avni, you're so boring. Just one sip, just to be one of us." I felt torn in two. I wanted to belong so badly. I also knew I didn't want it.

One night I said, very simply, "No, I don't drink. I'm going to sleep." No speech. One of them rolled her eyes. I went to bed early, heart thumping.

The next month I joined the college trekking club. On the first climb, a girl called Farida shared her water and said, "Good, someone who'll actually remember the view." We're still friends. Thirty years.

qa.a: She stayed in the hostel in Pune.

qa.q: How did young Avni feel when her roommates teased her?
qa.a: Young Avni felt torn, badly wanting to belong but knowing she did not want to drink.

qa.q: What choice inside the story made the biggest difference?
qa.a: Saying a simple no without a speech and then joining the trekking club, where Avni found people who liked her sober.

qa.q: How might Farida have seen Avni on that first climb?
qa.a: Farida seemed glad to meet someone who didn't drink, and saw Avni as good company rather than boring.

grounding: The elder's story shows a young woman pushed to drink to fit in who says a simple no, leaves early and finds friends who accept her sober.

The fest ended at eleven, but the last bus back to the village left at ten, and Harish had already missed it twice this semester. Behind the auditorium his friends were passing around a bottle.

"Harish, one drink. Don't be a grandmother." Everyone laughed. Someone pressed a paper cup into his hand.

He felt his face heat. These were the boys he'd eaten lunch with for a year. He didn't want to lose them, and he didn't want the drink.

"No, I'm fine. I've got the bus." He handed the cup back.

"Boring!"

"Yeah," he said, and smiled, and walked away.

At the bus stand he found Rekha from his statistics class, also waiting. "Escaped too?" she asked. They talked about the dance performance all the way home. Next week she invited him to the college photography club.

In Mahoba the tobacco shop owner knew everyone's mother, so it was only a matter of time. Saurabh came home from the bus depot to find Amma standing in the courtyard, the gutka packets from his cupboard in her fist.

"Two years at the polytechnic and this is what you learn?" she shouted. "Your grandfather's mouth, do you remember? Do you?"

He felt the wall behind his back. His first instinct was to say they weren't his. Kashish, his younger sister, watched from the doorway, eyes wide.

Then he saw Amma's hand shaking. She wasn't only angry. She was scared, remembering Nanaji's last months.

"They're mine," he said quietly. "I've tried to stop. I can't."

Amma sat down heavily on the step. After a long time she said, "Tomorrow we go to the health centre together." He nodded.

Thomas sat in the clinic corridor in Kochi, knee bouncing, the appointment slip damp in his hand. He'd booked it at 1 am, after waking on the bathroom floor, and had nearly cancelled twice since.

Dr Sudha had a quiet voice and a cluttered desk. "What brings you in?"

He had rehearsed the soft version on the bus. A few drinks at weekends, a bit of stress. His mouth opened to say it.

Instead he heard himself say, "Every night. Since my mother's surgery. I hide bottles in my college bag. Last week I woke on the floor."

The doctor didn't flinch. She asked more questions, wrote carefully, and said, "Thank you for telling me all of it. That makes it possible to help you." She gave him a referral to a counsellor and a follow-up date.

Outside, the rain had stopped. He felt shaky and oddly lighter.

qa.a: He booked it at 1 am, after waking on the bathroom floor.

qa.a: Thomas felt nervous, with his knee bouncing and the slip damp in his hand, and part of him wanted to cancel.

Fourth meeting. I spoke for the first time about the 3 am scrolling and the lectures I've missed since August. I thought they'd look at me like my family does, like I'm lazy. I'm Kamal, and I want to write down how it happened so I remember. It began with a free bonus on a cricket betting app during the inter-college cricket league. I won a little. Then I lost more than I'd won. By December I was awake at 2 am, phone brightness low so my roommate wouldn't wake, telling myself the next match would fix it.

One night I opened a chat to Pooja, my closest friend from school, to ask for a loan. I wrote, "Can you lend me something till next week?" My thumb stayed over the send button for a full minute.

I deleted it and called her instead, and told her everything. She stayed on the phone while I deleted the apps and set a block on my phone. The next day we found the student counselling service. The game, the counsellor said, is designed to keep you playing. That helped more than I expected.

On my 2 am round I found Kalyani in the common room, phone glowing, legs pulled up, eyes red. She jumped when I switched on the light and pushed the phone under a cushion.

I sat beside her and asked what was keeping her up. After a while she showed me. A betting app. She said she had been trying to win back what she lost last week, and the week before. She said, "If I win once I'll stop." Her voice was flat, tired.

At 8 am she called her mother, and I booked her a slot with the college counsellor for the same afternoon. I will check on her tonight.

Swati came to my room after dinner and sat on the floor instead of the bed. Then she said it: "I don't see the point of anything. I feel hopeless, Gopika. Don't tell anyone."

My heart was pounding. I wanted to say "don't think like that" but I didn't. I sat down next to her and asked her to tell me more. I listened. Then I asked her straight out if she had been thinking of ending her life. She said sometimes.

I told her I couldn't keep this secret, because I care about her too much. She cried, but she didn't leave. We called the helpline number from the notice board together, on speaker. Then we went down to the warden, who called the on-call counsellor, who talked to Swati for an hour.

In Dharampur, Pema had sat next to Lokesh on the school bus for ten years. Since his father's shop burned down in July, Lokesh had stopped coming to the tea stall, stopped answering calls, and stared at the ground in the college corridor.

Pema wanted to go to him. But every sentence Pema rehearsed sounded wrong. What if the words made it worse?

Bhavna, Pema's cousin, was shelling peas on the back step. "You're scared you'll say the wrong thing. So say a small true thing."

That evening Pema found Lokesh sitting alone behind the temple. Pema sat down and said only, "I'm here. I care about you. You don't have to be okay." Lokesh's face crumpled.

After a long silence, Pema said, "Let's talk to Sharma sir tomorrow. He runs the counselling hour." Lokesh nodded. The next morning they went together.

For five days Santiago avoided the university cafeteria in Córdoba, because Abebe would be there. Abebe had lost his scholarship the week before, and since then he'd gone grey and quiet, sleeping through classes. Santiago kept typing messages and deleting them. Everything sounded like a greeting card, or like a lecture. What if he said the wrong thing and Abebe shut down completely?

On Friday he saw Abebe alone on the library steps, and his feet carried him over before his fear could stop him.

"Hey. I'm sorry I disappeared. I didn't know what to say. I'm here. I care. Can we go and get some help together?"

Abebe looked at him for a long moment. "The counselling office closes at five."

It was four-fifteen. They walked there together, not talking much, and Santiago waited in the corridor until Abebe came out.

Ojas came in today, not for himself, he said, but about his roommate Divyansh, who has been low since his parents separated. For two months Ojas has been his only support: late-night talks, food runs, covering attendance. Today Ojas sat with his fists pressed into his knees.
